label: Half and full adders
lesson:
# Half and full adders

Binary addition is column addition with carries, and the full adder is one column. Every adder architecture, from the ripple-carry adder to the Kogge-Stone tree, is a different way of computing the same carries, and every multiplier is a pile of full adders. The generate and propagate signals introduced here are the vocabulary of all fast adders.

## Carries column by column

Adding $a$ and $b$ bit by bit, column $i$ receives $a_i$, $b_i$ and a carry-in $c_i$ from column $i - 1$ (with $c_0$ the adder's carry-in), and produces a sum bit and a carry-out $c_{i+1}$. The carry-out is 1 when at least two of the three inputs are 1.

Add $a = 01101011$ and $b = 00110110$ with $c_0 = 0$. Column 0: $1 + 0 = 1$, no carry. Column 1: $1 + 1 = 10$, carry into column 2. Column 2: $0 + 1 + 1$ carries again, and so does column 3 ($1 + 0 + 1$). Column 4: $0 + 1 + 1$ carries; column 5: $1 + 1 + 1 = 11$ carries; column 6: $1 + 0 + 1$ carries; column 7: $0 + 0 + 1$ does not. Six columns produce a carry, and the sum is 10100001 ($107 + 54 = 161$).

## Generate, propagate and the full adder equations

A half adder adds two bits: $s = a \oplus b$, $c = ab$. A full adder adds three:

$$s_i = a_i \oplus b_i \oplus c_i, \qquad c_{i+1} = a_i b_i + c_i (a_i \oplus b_i).$$

Name the two pieces: generate $g_i = a_i b_i$ (the column makes a carry by itself) and propagate $p_i = a_i \oplus b_i$ (the column passes an incoming carry through). Then $c_{i+1} = g_i + p_i c_i$ and $s_i = p_i \oplus c_i$. In the example above, columns 1 and 5 generate ($a_i = b_i = 1$), and columns 0, 2, 3, 4 and 6 propagate. A full adder is two half adders plus an OR gate: the first half adder produces $g_i$ and $p_i$, the second adds $c_i$.

## Gate counts and the cost of a column

Built from two half adders and an OR, a full adder uses 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR gate: 5 gates. An $n$-bit adder made of $n$ full adders therefore uses $5n$ gates; if the carry-in is known to be 0, the least significant column can be a half adder (2 gates), giving $5(n - 1) + 2$.

Real standard-cell libraries have dedicated full-adder cells (often a mirror adder in CMOS, about 28 transistors) that are smaller and faster than five separate gates, and synthesis tools map arithmetic onto them when it pays. More important for architecture is the structure of the carry path: in each column $c_{i+1}$ depends on $c_i$ through one AND-OR (or a majority gate), and how that dependence is chained across columns is what distinguishes the adders that follow.

## Going deeper

Harris and Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture" (2nd ed., 2012), section 5.2; Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed., 2010), section 11.2.

label: Ripple-carry adders
prereqs: Propagation delay through a gate network
lesson:
# Ripple-carry adders

The ripple-carry adder chains $n$ full adders, each carry-out feeding the next carry-in. It is the smallest adder and the slowest: its delay grows linearly with width. It is the baseline against which every faster adder is measured, and synthesis tools still choose it when timing allows, because area and power are lowest.

## The worst-case carry chain

In the worst case a carry generated in column 0 must ripple through every column to the top. Model each full adder's carry-out as settling $d_c$ gate delays after its carry-in (or after its operand inputs, for column 0, whose carry-in is ready at time 0), and its sum as settling $d_s$ gate delays after its carry-in. Then $c_{i+1}$ settles at $(i + 1) d_c$, the carry-out of an $n$-bit adder at $n\,d_c$, and the most significant sum bit at

$$t_{s_{n-1}} = (n - 1)\, d_c + d_s.$$

With $d_c = 2$ and $d_s = 2$, a 32-bit ripple adder's top sum settles after $62 + 2 = 64$ gate delays, and its carry-out after 64.

## Converting to time and sizing to a budget

Gate delays become time once a technology is fixed. If a gate delay is 15 ps, the 32-bit adder above takes $64 \cdot 15 = 960$ ps, too slow for a 1 GHz clock once register overhead is added.

Turn the formula around to find the widest ripple adder that fits a budget $B$: the largest $n$ with $(n - 1) d_c + d_s \le B$. With $d_c = 2$, $d_s = 3$ and a budget of 40 gate delays, $(n - 1) \cdot 2 \le 37$ gives $n = 19$. Synthesis tools make exactly this kind of decision when they pick an adder implementation per instance: ripple where the slack allows, a faster structure where it does not.

## Average versus worst case

The worst case is rare for random operands. A carry ripples only through a run of propagate columns ($a_i \ne b_i$) that starts at a generating column. For uniformly random operands the expected longest such run is about $\log_2 n$, so a typical addition settles long before the worst case.

Synchronous design cannot exploit this: the clock period must cover the worst case, because any operand pair might occur and static timing analysis is input-independent. Self-timed adders with completion detection do exploit it, at the cost of extra logic and an asynchronous handshake. In synchronous logic the response is architectural: shorten the worst-case carry path itself, which is what carry-lookahead, carry-select and prefix adders do.

label: Carry-lookahead adders
lesson:
# Carry-lookahead adders

A carry-lookahead adder computes carries directly from generate and propagate signals instead of waiting for them to ripple. Unrolling the carry recurrence gives two-level logic for each carry, and grouping bits into blocks with group generate and group propagate keeps the gates small. It is the conceptual bridge from the ripple adder to parallel-prefix adders.

## Generate and propagate per bit

Every column computes $g_i = a_i b_i$ and $p_i = a_i \oplus b_i$ in one gate delay, independent of every other column. For $a = 10110110$ and $b = 01100101$, the generate vector $a \mathbin{\&} b = 00100100$ has 2 set bits and the propagate vector $a \oplus b = 11010011$ has 5.

No column has both bits set, because $g_i = 1$ requires $a_i = b_i$ and $p_i = 1$ requires $a_i \ne b_i$. Columns with neither are kill columns ($a_i = b_i = 0$): they absorb any incoming carry. Every fast adder starts from these two vectors; only how it combines them differs.

## Unrolling the carry recurrence

Substituting $c_{i+1} = g_i + p_i c_i$ into itself gives each carry as a sum of products of $g$, $p$ and $c_0$:

$$c_1 = g_0 + p_0 c_0,\quad c_2 = g_1 + p_1 g_0 + p_1 p_0 c_0,$$
$$c_4 = g_3 + p_3 g_2 + p_3 p_2 g_1 + p_3 p_2 p_1 g_0 + p_3 p_2 p_1 p_0 c_0.$$

Each carry is a two-level AND-OR function, so all four carries of a 4-bit block are ready two gate delays after $g$, $p$ and $c_0$. With $g_3..g_0 = 0010$, $p_3..p_0 = 1101$ and $c_0 = 1$: $c_1 = 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1$, $c_2 = 1$ (from $g_1$), $c_3 = 0 + p_2 c_2 = 1$, $c_4 = 0 + p_3 c_3 = 1$. The carry vector $c_4 c_3 c_2 c_1 = 1111$.

## Blocks and their delay

The product terms grow quickly (the carry out of an $n$-bit block has $n + 1$ terms with up to $n + 1$ inputs), so lookahead logic is limited to blocks of about 4 bits. Each block also produces a group generate $G = g_3 + p_3 g_2 + p_3 p_2 g_1 + p_3 p_2 p_1 g_0$ and a group propagate $P = p_3 p_2 p_1 p_0$, so its carry-out is $G + P c_{in}$.

If blocks are rippled, a 16-bit adder of four 4-bit blocks has this delay under a simple model: $g, p$ take 1 gate delay; each block produces its carries 2 gate delays after its carry-in (its $G$ and $P$ are ready earlier); sums take 1 more XOR delay. Block 1 finishes at $1 + 2 = 3$, block $k$ at $2k + 1$, and the last sums at $2 \cdot 4 + 2 = 10$ gate delays, against $2 \cdot 15 + 2 = 32$ for a ripple adder with $d_c = d_s = 2$. Applying lookahead recursively to the block $G$ and $P$ signals gives logarithmic depth, which is the parallel-prefix idea.

label: Carry-select and carry-skip adders
lesson:
# Carry-select and carry-skip adders

Two classic tricks speed up an adder without full lookahead. A carry-select adder computes each block's sum twice, once for each possible carry-in, and picks the right one with a mux when the real carry arrives. A carry-skip adder lets a carry jump over a block whose bits all propagate. Both trade area for delay, and both have an optimal block size that is a nice small optimization problem.

## Speculate both carries, then select

Split an $n$-bit adder into blocks of $k$ bits. The first block is an ordinary ripple adder. Every other block contains two ripple adders, one assuming carry-in 0 and one assuming carry-in 1, plus muxes. All blocks compute in parallel and finish at $k\, t_c$. The real carry then passes from block to block through one mux each:

$$t = k\, t_c + \left(\frac{n}{k} - 1\right) t_{mux}.$$

For $n = 32$, $k = 8$, $t_c = 2$ and $t_{mux} = 2$ gate delays: $16 + 3 \cdot 2 = 22$ gate delays to the carry-out, against 64 for the ripple adder. The cost is nearly double the adder area. This is Shannon expansion on the carry-in: each block computes both cofactors and the mux chooses.

## Choosing the block size

The delay $k\, t_c + (n/k - 1) t_{mux}$ has two competing terms: bigger blocks ripple longer, smaller blocks need more muxes. Treating $k$ as continuous, the minimum is at $k^* = \sqrt{n\, t_{mux} / t_c}$, giving delay $O(\sqrt{n})$.

For $n = 64$ with $t_c = t_{mux} = 2$, the divisors of 64 give: $k = 4$: $8 + 15 \cdot 2 = 38$; $k = 8$: $16 + 7 \cdot 2 = 30$; $k = 16$: $32 + 3 \cdot 2 = 38$. The best uniform block is $k = 8 = \sqrt{64}$, at 30 gate delays. Non-uniform blocks do better: since later blocks have longer to compute before their select arrives, they can be larger (block sizes growing 1, 2, 3, ...), which is the square-root carry-select adder.

## Carry-skip

A carry-skip (carry-bypass) adder adds a mux per block that forwards the block's carry-in directly to its carry-out when every bit in the block propagates ($P = p_{k-1} \cdots p_0 = 1$). In the worst case, a carry generated in the first block ripples through it, skips every middle block, and ripples through the last:

$$t \approx k\, t_c + \left(\frac{n}{k} - 2\right) t_{skip} + k\, t_c.$$

With $n = 32$, $k = 4$, $t_c = 2$, $t_{skip} = 2$: $8 + 6 \cdot 2 + 8 = 28$ gate delays. Carry-skip costs much less area than carry-select (one mux and an AND per block), but its delay is harder for a static timer to see: the long ripple path through every block exists structurally but cannot be sensitized, a false path. Without false-path handling the timer reports the pessimistic ripple delay.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Parallel-prefix adders

Every carry is a prefix of the generate-propagate sequence combined by one associative operator. That observation turns carry computation into the parallel-prefix problem, solvable in logarithmic depth, and it produces the whole family of fast adders used in processors: Sklansky, Kogge-Stone, Brent-Kung, Han-Carlson, Ladner-Fischer. Datapath synthesis tools choose among these structures per adder.

## The prefix operator

Define the span signals $(G_{i:j}, P_{i:j})$: the span of bits $j$ to $i$ generates a carry, or propagates one through. Two adjacent spans combine with the operator

$$(G_{hi}, P_{hi}) \circ (G_{lo}, P_{lo}) = (G_{hi} + P_{hi} G_{lo},\; P_{hi} P_{lo}).$$

The operator is associative (though not commutative), so the span $i{:}0$ can be built from any bracketing of the single-bit spans $(g_k, p_k)$. With carry-in 0, the carry into bit $i + 1$ is $c_{i+1} = G_{i:0}$, and the sum is $s_i = p_i \oplus G_{i-1:0}$. Associativity is the whole trick: it lets a tree evaluate all $n$ prefixes in $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ levels instead of a chain of $n$.

## Computing the prefix generates

For a concrete pair of operands the prefix generates are just the carries. Take $a = 10110110$, $b = 01100101$ (8 bits) with carry-in 0. The carries computed column by column are $c_1 = 0$, $c_2 = 0$, $c_3 = 1$, $c_4 = 0$, $c_5 = 0$, $c_6 = 1$, $c_7 = 1$, $c_8 = 1$, so $G_{i:0} = 1$ for $i = 2, 5, 6, 7$: four of the eight prefixes.

The tree computes exactly these values, only faster. For example $G_{7:4}$ and $G_{3:0}$ combine as $G_{7:0} = G_{7:4} + P_{7:4} G_{3:0}$. Here $G_{3:0} = 0$ (no carry leaves the low nibble) but $G_{7:4} = 1$ (bit 5 generates and bits 6 and 7 propagate), so $G_{7:0} = 1$.

## Depth, size and fanout

Any prefix network on $n$ inputs needs at least $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ levels, since the top output depends on all $n$ inputs through two-input nodes. Networks differ in node count, fanout and wiring at a given depth.

The Sklansky (divide-and-conquer) network reaches minimum depth with $\frac{n}{2}\log_2 n$ nodes, but at its last level one node drives $n/2$ others, a large fanout that needs buffering. For $n = 32$ that is $16 \cdot 5 = 80$ nodes in 5 levels, with a fanout of 16 at the final level. Kogge-Stone keeps fanout at 2 by using more nodes and long wires; Brent-Kung uses fewer nodes at nearly twice the depth. Choosing among them is a trade between logic depth, area, fanout and wiring congestion, which is why it is decided late, with physical information.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Kogge-Stone versus Brent-Kung

Kogge-Stone and Brent-Kung are the two ends of the prefix-adder design space. Kogge-Stone has minimum depth and fanout 2 but many nodes and long wires. Brent-Kung has nearly the minimum possible node count but almost twice the depth. Counting their nodes and levels exactly is the basis for any architecture comparison, whether by a human, a datapath synthesizer, or an agent exploring the space.

## Kogge-Stone: minimum depth, fanout two

In Kogge-Stone, at level $\ell = 0, 1, \dots, \log_2 n - 1$, every position $i \ge 2^\ell$ combines its current span with the span ending at $i - 2^\ell$. Level $\ell$ therefore has $n - 2^\ell$ nodes, and the total is

$$\sum_{\ell=0}^{\log_2 n - 1} (n - 2^\ell) = n \log_2 n - n + 1.$$

For $n = 16$: depth 4 and $64 - 16 + 1 = 49$ nodes. Every node drives at most two others, so no buffering is needed, but the wire from position $i - 2^\ell$ to $i$ spans $2^\ell$ bit pitches, so the last level has wires reaching half the adder's width. Wiring, not logic, is Kogge-Stone's cost.

## Brent-Kung: few nodes, twice the depth

Brent-Kung computes the prefixes in two sweeps. The up-sweep builds a binary tree over the inputs: $n/2 + n/4 + \dots + 1 = n - 1$ nodes in $\log_2 n$ levels, producing the prefixes at positions $2^k - 1$. The down-sweep fills in the remaining prefixes with $n - 1 - \log_2 n$ nodes in $\log_2 n - 1$ levels. Totals:

$$\text{nodes} = 2n - 2 - \log_2 n, \qquad \text{depth} = 2\log_2 n - 1.$$

For $n = 16$: 26 nodes in 7 levels, against Kogge-Stone's 49 nodes in 4 levels. Fanout stays at most 2 and wires are short, so Brent-Kung is attractive when timing is loose and area or power matters.

## Comparing the two

At $n = 64$, Kogge-Stone has depth 6 and $384 - 64 + 1 = 321$ nodes; Brent-Kung has depth 11 and $128 - 2 - 6 = 120$ nodes, a difference of 201 nodes for 5 extra levels. If each level costs one prefix-node delay, the Kogge-Stone adder is almost twice as fast in logic, but its long wires add RC delay that the node count does not show, and its area and power are more than double.

Intermediate networks interpolate: Han-Carlson runs Kogge-Stone on odd positions only and adds one level to fix the even ones; Ladner-Fischer and Knowles families trade fanout against node count. Datapath synthesis typically starts from a fast structure and relaxes it where slack allows. Comparing candidates on depth and node count alone is a fast first filter; only placement and routing reveal the wire cost.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Subtractors and comparators

An adder becomes a subtractor by inverting one operand and setting the carry-in, because $a - b = a + \bar{b} + 1$ modulo $2^n$. The carry-out and the overflow and sign flags of that subtraction then answer every comparison, signed or unsigned. ALUs implement comparison this way, and so do the condition codes a processor's branch logic reads.

## Subtraction with an adder

Since $\bar{b} + 1 \equiv -b \pmod{2^n}$, feeding $\bar{b}$ into an adder with carry-in 1 computes $a - b \bmod 2^n$. An adder-subtractor puts an XOR gate on each $b$ input, controlled by a subtract signal that also drives the carry-in.

For 8-bit $a = 75$, $b = 200$: $\bar{b} = 55$, and $75 + 55 + 1 = 131$. As an unsigned result that is $(75 - 200) \bmod 256 = 131$. A signed reading sees the same input pattern of $b$ as -56 and the same output pattern as $131 - 256 = -125$, the wrapped result of $75 - (-56) = 131$, a signed overflow. The bit pattern is the same either way; only the interpretation, and the flags, differ.

## Unsigned comparison from the carry-out

The carry-out $c_n$ of $a + \bar{b} + 1$ is 1 exactly when $a \ge b$ as unsigned numbers. The reason: the adder computes $a + (2^n - 1 - b) + 1 = 2^n + (a - b)$, which reaches $2^n$ (setting the carry-out) iff $a - b \ge 0$.

So the carry-out is an inverted borrow: $c_n = 0$ means the subtraction borrowed, $a < b$. For $a = 75$, $b = 200$ the true sum is $75 + 55 + 1 = 131 < 256$, so $c_n = 0$ and $a < b$. Processor flag conventions differ on whether they store $c_n$ or its complement as the carry flag after a subtraction, a detail an instruction-set simulator and the RTL must agree on.

## Signed comparison from N and V

For signed operands the sign of the result is not enough, because the subtraction can overflow. The rule is

$$a < b \iff N \oplus V = 1,$$

where $N$ is the result's sign bit and $V$ is the signed-overflow flag. Take 8-bit $a = 100$, $b = -50$: $a - b = 150$ overflows to -106, so $N = 1$ but $V = 1$, and $N \oplus V = 0$, correctly saying $a \ge b$. Without the overflow correction the sign bit alone would claim $100 < -50$.

An equality comparator needs no subtraction at all: $a = b$ iff every bit of $a \oplus b$ is 0, an XOR row followed by a NOR tree of depth $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Multiplier architectures

A multiplier forms partial products and adds them. Every architecture follows the same three steps: generate partial products, reduce them to two rows, and add the two rows with a fast carry-propagate adder. Architectures differ in how many partial products they create (Booth recoding) and how they reduce them (arrays, Wallace and Dadda trees). Multipliers dominate area in DSP and machine-learning accelerators.

## Partial products

Multiplying an $n$-bit unsigned multiplicand $A$ by an $m$-bit multiplier $B$ by long multiplication creates one row per multiplier bit: row $j$ is $A \cdot b_j$ shifted left by $j$, so its value is $b_j \cdot A \cdot 2^j$. Each partial-product bit is one AND gate, $a_i b_j$.

With $A = 1011$ (11) and $B = 1101$ (13), the rows are 1011 (row 0), 0 (row 1, since $b_1 = 0$), $1011 \ll 2 = 44$ (row 2) and $1011 \ll 3 = 88$ (row 3). Their sum is $11 + 44 + 88 = 143 = 11 \cdot 13$. The multiplication is now an addition problem: summing $m$ shifted rows.

## Sizes and widths

An $n \times m$ unsigned multiplier has $n m$ partial-product bits, so $n m$ AND gates, arranged in $m$ rows. The product needs $n + m$ bits: the largest product is $(2^n - 1)(2^m - 1) < 2^{n+m}$. A $16 \times 16$ multiplier has 256 partial-product bits and a 32-bit product.

For two's-complement operands the product of an $n$-bit and an $m$-bit signed number also fits in $n + m$ bits; the extreme case is $(-2^{n-1})(-2^{m-1}) = 2^{n+m-2}$, which needs the full $n + m$ bits as a positive signed value. Signed partial products require sign extension or the Baugh-Wooley rearrangement, which complements selected partial-product bits and adds constants so that every row stays positive.

## Array versus tree reduction

An array multiplier adds the rows one at a time with a grid of full adders, each row's adders taking the previous row's sums and carries. It is regular and easy to lay out, but its critical path grows linearly with the operand width, roughly two full-adder delays per bit for an $n \times n$ array, and its many unequal paths produce heavy glitching.

A tree multiplier instead reduces all rows in parallel with carry-save adders: a row of full adders takes three rows and produces two (a sum row and a carry row shifted left), without propagating any carry. The number of rows shrinks by a factor of about $3/2$ per level, so reduction takes $O(\log n)$ levels, followed by one fast carry-propagate adder. Wallace and Dadda trees are the two standard schedules for this reduction, and radix-4 Booth recoding halves the number of rows before it starts.

## Going deeper

Parhami, "Computer Arithmetic: Algorithms and Hardware Designs" (2nd ed., 2010), chapters 9 to 12; Baugh and Wooley, "A Two's Complement Parallel Array Multiplication Algorithm" (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1973).

label: Radix-4 Booth recoding
lesson:
# Radix-4 Booth recoding

Radix-4 (modified) Booth recoding rewrites a two's-complement multiplier in base 4 with digits from $\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$. Each digit selects a partial product that is a trivial multiple of the multiplicand (zero, plus or minus itself, plus or minus twice itself), and the number of partial products halves. Nearly every high-performance multiplier uses it.

## Half as many partial products

A radix-2 multiplier creates one partial product per multiplier bit: $n$ rows for an $n$-bit multiplier. Radix-4 Booth examines the multiplier two bits at a time with one bit of overlap and creates one partial product per pair. For an $n$-bit two's-complement multiplier with $n$ even, that is $n/2$ partial products.

A $16 \times 16$ signed multiplier drops from 16 rows to 8; a $54 \times 54$ (double-precision significand) from 54 to 27. Each Booth row is a little wider, since it may hold $2A$, and needs a sign-handling bit, but halving the rows shrinks the reduction tree by about a level and saves substantial area.

## The recoding rule

Append $y_{-1} = 0$ below the multiplier's least significant bit. Digit $i$ ($i = 0, \dots, n/2 - 1$) looks at bits $y_{2i+1}, y_{2i}, y_{2i-1}$:

$$d_i = -2 y_{2i+1} + y_{2i} + y_{2i-1}.$$

So the triplet 000 or 111 gives 0, 001 and 010 give $+1$, 011 gives $+2$, 100 gives -2, and 101 and 110 give -1. Recode the 8-bit $y = 01101110$ (110): triplets from the bottom are $(y_1 y_0 y_{-1}) = 100 \to -2$, $(y_3 y_2 y_1) = 111 \to 0$, $(y_5 y_4 y_3) = 101 \to -1$, $(y_7 y_6 y_5) = 011 \to 2$. Check: $-2 + 0 \cdot 4 - 1 \cdot 16 + 2 \cdot 64 = 110$.

## Selecting and negating multiples

Digit $d_i$ selects the partial product $d_i \cdot A$, shifted left by $2i$ bits. With $A = 13$ and the digits above, the partial products are -26, 0, $-13 \cdot 16$ and $26 \cdot 64$; their sum is $13 \cdot 110 = 1430$.

Every multiple is cheap: $A$ is a wire, $2A$ a one-bit shift, and a negative multiple is the bitwise inverse plus one. The "plus one" is not added immediately; it is placed as an extra bit in the reduction tree so no carry chain is needed per row. The sign of each row is handled by a few extra bits rather than full sign extension. Booth's subtlety for verification is that the partial products no longer correspond to multiplier bits, so a word-level equivalence checker or an algebraic method must reason about the recoded sum rather than the original bit structure.

## Going deeper

Booth, "A Signed Binary Multiplication Technique" (Quarterly Journal of Mechanics and Applied Mathematics, 1951); MacSorley, "High-Speed Arithmetic in Binary Computers" (Proceedings of the IRE, 1961); Parhami, "Computer Arithmetic" (2nd ed., 2010), chapter 10.

label: Wallace and Dadda trees
lesson:
# Wallace and Dadda trees

A Wallace or Dadda tree reduces a matrix of partial-product bits to two rows using full adders (3:2 counters) and half adders, with no carry propagation, so the reduction takes logarithmically many levels. Wallace reduces as aggressively as possible at every level; Dadda reduces as little as possible while keeping to the same number of levels, which saves adders. Counting levels and adders is how multiplier architectures are compared.

## Levels of 3:2 reduction

A full adder takes three bits of one column and emits a sum bit in that column and a carry bit in the next. Applied across the matrix, each level turns every group of three rows into two, so a height of $r$ becomes $2\lfloor r/3 \rfloor + (r \bmod 3)$, which equals $\lceil 2r/3 \rceil$.

Dadda states the same schedule from the bottom: the maximum heights that can be reduced to 2 in $j$ levels are $d_1 = 2$, $d_{j+1} = \lfloor 1.5\, d_j \rfloor$, giving $2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 28, 42, 63, \dots$. The number of levels for height $r$ is the number of terms of this sequence below $r$. An $8 \times 8$ multiplier has maximum column height 8, and $2, 3, 4, 6 < 8$, so 4 levels; a $32 \times 32$ multiplier needs 8 levels.

## Counting Dadda's adders

Every full adder takes in three bits and emits two, so it removes exactly one bit from the matrix; a half adder takes two and emits two, removing none (it only moves a bit to the next column). An $n \times n$ multiplier starts with $n^2$ bits. Dadda's minimal-reduction rule yields closed forms (Townsend, Swartzlander and Abraham): an $n \times n$ Dadda tree uses

$$n^2 - 4n + 3 \text{ full adders and } n - 1 \text{ half adders},$$

followed by a $(2n - 2)$-bit carry-propagate adder. For $n = 8$: 35 full adders and 7 half adders. A Wallace tree for the same multiplier has the same number of levels but uses more half adders, because it reduces every column eagerly.

## Booth recoding meets the tree

Radix-4 Booth recoding halves the number of rows, so a $32 \times 32$ multiplier presents about 16 rows (plus the bits that complete the negations) instead of 32. The Dadda count drops from 8 levels (for height 32) to 6 (for height 16: the terms 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 13 lie below 16). Each level costs one full-adder delay, about two gate delays, so Booth saves about four gate delays here, against the cost of the Booth encoders and partial-product muxes.

4:2 compressors, built from two full adders but with a carry path designed to stay inside the cell, reduce four rows to two per level, so they halve the height each level and give a more regular tree. Whether Booth plus a Dadda tree, or a plain array, or 4:2 compressors win depends on the target's timing, area and wiring, a classic space for automated design exploration.

## Going deeper

Wallace, "A Suggestion for a Fast Multiplier" (IEEE Transactions on Electronic Computers, 1964); Dadda, "Some Schemes for Parallel Multipliers" (Alta Frequenza, 1965); Townsend, Swartzlander and Abraham, "A Comparison of Dadda and Wallace Multiplier Delays" (SPIE, 2003).

label: SRAM organization
lesson:
# SRAM organization

Static RAM is the on-chip memory of caches, buffers and register files, and in many chips it occupies more area than logic. It is never built as a logical $W \times B$ array directly: the bits are folded into a physical array whose shape is chosen for speed and area, with a row decoder, column multiplexers and sense amplifiers. Memory compilers generate these macros, and floorplanning, timing and power tools treat them as hard blocks whose geometry follows from the organization.

## The 6T cell and the array

The standard SRAM cell is six transistors: two cross-coupled inverters hold the bit, and two access transistors connect the storage nodes to a complementary pair of bitlines when the row's wordline is raised. A $W$-word by $B$-bit memory stores $W B$ bits, so $6 W B$ transistors in the cell array alone; a 32 KB cache data array (262,144 bits) holds about 1.57 million cell transistors.

The cells sit in a grid of rows and columns. One wordline per row selects a row; every cell in that row drives its column's bitlines. The row decoder (an address decoder) turns part of the address into the one-hot wordline.

## Column multiplexing

A $1024 \times 32$ memory laid out as 1024 rows of 32 cells is tall and thin: long bitlines (slow, high capacitance) and a narrow array. Instead, put $m$ words in each physical row and select among them with a column multiplexer. The array then has

$$\text{rows} = \frac{W}{m}, \qquad \text{columns} = B\, m.$$

With $m = 4$: 256 rows by 128 columns. The address splits accordingly: $\log_2(W/m)$ bits drive the row decoder and $\log_2 m$ bits drive the column mux. Here 8 row-address bits and 2 column-address bits make up the 10-bit word address.

## Choosing the shape

The column-mux factor $m$ is chosen to make the array close to square, which balances wordline length (RC delay across a row) against bitline length (the load each cell must discharge). The array is square when $W/m = B m$, that is $m = \sqrt{W/B}$. For $4096 \times 16$, $m = \sqrt{256} = 16$, giving 256 rows by 256 columns.

Large memories are further split into banks or sub-arrays, each with local decoders and sense amplifiers, because a single huge array would have unacceptably long lines. Memory compilers expose words, bits, mux factor and banking as parameters and emit the layout, a timing model and an abstract view; choosing among their configurations for a given timing and area target is routine design-space exploration.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed., 2010), chapter 12; Rabaey, Chandrakasan and Nikolic, "Digital Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2003), chapter 12.

lesson:
# DRAM refresh, bandwidth and latency

Dynamic RAM stores each bit as charge on a capacitor behind one transistor, which makes it far denser than SRAM but leaky and slow to access. DRAM lives off-chip (or stacked, as HBM), and a memory controller on the chip schedules its commands. The controller and PHY are standard blocks in a modern SoC, and their performance arithmetic (refresh overhead, peak bandwidth, row-buffer latency) drives system architecture.

## The 1T1C cell and refresh

A DRAM cell is one access transistor and one capacitor. Reading shares the cell's charge with a long bitline, and the sense amplifier detects a small voltage change, so a read is destructive and the row must be written back. The stored charge also leaks away, so every row must be refreshed within a retention window, conventionally 64 ms at normal temperature for DDR devices.

If the controller must issue $R$ refresh commands evenly over the window, the interval between commands is $t_{REFI} = 64\ \text{ms} / R$. With $R = 8192$, $t_{REFI} = 7.8125\ \mu\text{s}$. During each refresh the device is busy for $t_{RFC}$, so refresh costs a fraction $t_{RFC}/t_{REFI}$ of the time; with $t_{RFC} = 350$ ns that is about 4.5%. Denser devices have longer $t_{RFC}$, and refresh overhead grows with capacity.

## Peak bandwidth

A DDR interface transfers data on both clock edges. Its peak bandwidth is the bus width times the transfer rate:

$$BW = \frac{\text{width (bits)} \times \text{rate (MT/s)}}{8}\ \text{MB/s}.$$

A 64-bit DDR4-3200 channel (3200 mega-transfers per second) peaks at $64 \cdot 3200 / 8 = 25600$ MB/s, 25.6 GB/s. Sustained bandwidth is lower because of refresh, row changes, bus turnarounds between reads and writes, and bank conflicts; controller scheduling (for example open-row-first policies) exists to recover as much of the peak as possible.

## Row hits, misses and conflicts

Each bank has a row buffer holding one open row. An access to the open row is a row hit and costs the column latency $t_{CL}$. An access to a bank with no open row needs an activate first: $t_{RCD} + t_{CL}$. An access to a different row than the one open (a conflict) must precharge first: $t_{RP} + t_{RCD} + t_{CL}$.

With $t_{CL} = t_{RCD} = t_{RP} = 14$ ns, a hit costs 14 ns and a conflict 42 ns. If 70% of accesses hit and the rest conflict, the expected latency is $0.7 \cdot 14 + 0.3 \cdot 42 = 22.4$ ns. This expected-value calculation is the core of memory-controller policy: keeping rows open helps workloads with locality and hurts random ones, and address mapping (which address bits select bank, row and column) is chosen to spread conflicts across banks.

## Going deeper

Jacob, Ng and Wang, "Memory Systems: Cache, DRAM, Disk" (2008); JEDEC Standard JESD79-4 (DDR4 SDRAM).

label: Register files and ports
lesson:
# Register files and ports

A register file is a small, fast, heavily multi-ported memory: a processor reads two operands and writes one result per instruction, and a superscalar core does that for several instructions per cycle. Ports, not bits, dominate its cost. Register files are generated by memory compilers or built from flip-flops and muxes by synthesis, and choosing between the two is a recurring physical-design decision.

## Ports from the instruction mix

Each instruction of a typical RISC machine reads up to two source registers and writes one destination. A core that issues $w$ instructions per cycle needs $2w$ read ports and $w$ write ports to avoid structural conflicts. A 4-wide core needs 8 read and 4 write ports, 12 in all.

Each read port has its own address decoder and output mux; each write port has its own decoder and write drivers. With $R$ registers, every port takes a $\log_2 R$-bit address: a 64-entry, 12-port file decodes $12 \times 6 = 72$ address bits every cycle. Designers cut port counts with banking, port sharing or clustering of the execution units, accepting occasional stalls.

## Why area grows quadratically

In a multi-ported cell, each port adds a wordline (running horizontally) and at least one bitline (running vertically). If a cell needs a base of $a$ wire tracks in each direction plus one per port, its side grows as $a + p$ and its area as $(a + p)^2$.

With $a = 2$, going from 3 ports to 12 ports multiplies cell area by $(14/5)^2 = 7.84$. The longer wires also slow every access, so a heavily ported file is both large and slow. This is the physical reason wide superscalar cores split their register files, and why synthesis of a large many-ported register file from flip-flops quickly becomes routing-dominated.

## Write-before-read and bypassing

A register file written and read in the same cycle needs a rule. A common one is to write in the first half of the cycle and read in the second, so an instruction reading a register sees a value written by an instruction three stages ahead in the same cycle. That timing trick is what lets the classic five-stage pipeline avoid one stall cycle.

Values produced but not yet written are delivered by bypass (forwarding) paths that route an ALU result straight to the next instruction's inputs, around the register file. With issue width $w$ and $k$ bypassed stages, each operand mux chooses among roughly $1 + w k$ sources, and the bypass network, not the file itself, often becomes the critical path. Microarchitecture, register-file design and timing closure meet here.

## Going deeper

Rixner et al., "Register Organization for Media Processing" (HPCA, 2000); Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (6th ed., 2017), appendix C.

label: Content-addressable memories
lesson:
# Content-addressable memories

A content-addressable memory (CAM) inverts the usual interface: give it data and it returns the addresses where that data is stored, comparing every entry in parallel. Ternary CAMs (TCAMs) add a don't-care state per bit. They implement translation lookaside buffers, fully associative cache tags, and the longest-prefix-match tables of network routers, at a high price in area and power.

## Parallel match

Every CAM entry has a comparator on every bit. A search drives the key onto search lines running through all entries; each entry's match line stays high only if every bit matches. A binary CAM with $E$ entries of $W$ bits performs $E W$ bit comparisons per search, in one cycle. That parallelism is the point, and also the cost: every search charges every match line, so CAM search energy grows with the whole array.

A ternary entry stores 0, 1 or X (don't care) per bit, using two storage bits per cell, so a TCAM with $E$ entries of $W$ ternary bits stores $2 E W$ bits. An entry matches a key when every non-X bit equals the key bit. For key 1011, entry 1X11 matches, entry 10X0 does not (its last bit is 0), and entry XXXX matches anything.

## Priority among multiple matches

In a TCAM several entries can match. A priority encoder on the match lines picks one, conventionally the lowest-indexed match, and the entries are stored in priority order. For entries 0: 0XX1, 1: 10X1, 2: 1XX1, 3: XXXX with key 1011, entries 1, 2 and 3 match and the result is entry 1.

Routers use exactly this for longest-prefix match: store routes sorted by prefix length, longest first, with the unspecified low bits as X, so the first match is the most specific route, and a catch-all default route at the end matches everything. Inserting a route must preserve the order, which is why TCAM table management is a software problem in its own right.

## Cost and alternatives

A CAM cell needs storage plus comparison logic, so it is several times larger than an SRAM cell, and a TCAM cell larger again; search energy scales with entries times width. That limits CAMs to small, latency-critical structures: TLBs with tens to a few thousand entries, associative tag arrays, and router tables.

The alternative is hashing into an SRAM, which is denser and lower power but has variable latency and collisions. Set-associative caches are a middle point: a few ways compared in parallel, selected by an index. Choosing among CAM, hashed SRAM and set-associative structures is a classic microarchitecture trade-off, and memory compilers offer CAM macros alongside SRAM for that reason.

## Going deeper

Pagiamtzis and Sheikholeslami, "Content-Addressable Memory (CAM) Circuits and Architectures: A Tutorial and Survey" (IEEE JSSC, 2006).

label: Memory macros and non-volatile memory
lesson:
# Memory macros and non-volatile memory

Memories are not synthesized gate by gate. They arrive as macros produced by a memory compiler: a layout, a timing model, an abstract placement view and a behavioral model, all for a specific configuration. Non-volatile memories (flash, and emerging resistive and magnetic types) extend the family when data must survive power-down. A tool designer needs to know what each view promises and what each technology trades.

## What a memory compiler delivers

Given words, bits, column-mux factor, banking and options such as write masks or redundancy, a memory compiler emits a hard macro with a set of views: the layout (GDSII or OASIS), an abstract physical view (LEF) with pin locations and blockages for placement and routing, a timing and power model (Liberty) characterized at each corner, and a behavioral Verilog model for simulation.

Implementation tools never look inside the macro; they place it as a block, route to its pins and time it through its Liberty arcs (clock-to-output for reads, setup and hold on address and data inputs). The macro's correctness inside is the compiler vendor's responsibility, verified by its own characterization.

## Test and repair

Memories have the densest layout on the chip and therefore the most defects. They are tested by memory built-in self-test (MBIST): an on-chip engine runs march algorithms (sequences of writes and reads in ascending and descending address order) that detect stuck-at, transition and coupling faults.

Large memories also carry redundant rows and columns. When MBIST finds a failing row, built-in self-repair or fuse programming remaps it to a spare, raising yield substantially. The redundancy, the repair logic and the BIST controller are all inserted by the flow, which is why memory macros come with their own test views and why design-for-test tools must understand them.

## Non-volatile memories

Embedded flash stores charge on a floating gate or in a charge-trap layer; it retains data for years without power, but writes are slow, need high voltage and wear the cell out after a limited number of program and erase cycles, and it needs extra process steps. Emerging non-volatile memories store state differently: MRAM in the magnetization of a magnetic tunnel junction, ReRAM in a resistive filament, phase-change memory in the crystalline or amorphous state of a chalcogenide. They write faster than flash and integrate in the back-end metal layers, at the price of variability and sensing difficulty.

Read-only memory (mask ROM) is fixed at fabrication. For a designer the choice is a matrix of density, endurance, write energy, retention, process cost and read speed, and the macro's views (timing, power, test) differ accordingly.

## Going deeper

label: Datapath and control
lesson:
# Datapath and control

A processor, and most accelerators, splits into a datapath, which holds and transforms data (registers, ALUs, shifters, muxes, memories), and a control unit, which decides each cycle what the datapath does by driving its mux selects, register enables and operation codes. This split is how RTL is organized, how high-level synthesis builds hardware from a schedule, and how verification divides its effort.

## Datapath elements and control signals

The datapath is built from the components of the earlier subdomains: a register file, an ALU (adder, logic unit, shifter, comparator), multiplexers that route operands, and memory interfaces. Every mux select, register write enable, ALU operation code and memory read or write strobe is a control signal.

For one instruction, say `add r3, r1, r2`, control must select the register-file read addresses, set the ALU to add, route the ALU result (not the memory data) to the register file's write port, and enable the write to r3. A different instruction is a different setting of the same control signals on the same datapath.

## Single-cycle and multicycle control

In a single-cycle design every instruction completes in one long clock cycle, and control is pure combinational decoding of the instruction. The cycle must fit the slowest instruction (typically a load: instruction fetch, register read, address add, data memory, register write), so every other instruction wastes time.

A multicycle design breaks each instruction into steps of one short cycle each, reusing units across steps (one memory for instructions and data, one ALU for address and arithmetic). Control becomes a finite-state machine whose states are the steps, and instructions take different numbers of cycles. Pipelining then overlaps those steps across instructions. High-level synthesis builds the same structure automatically: its schedule assigns operations to control steps, its binding shares units, and its controller is an FSM.

## Hardwired versus microcoded control

Control can be hardwired, synthesized logic and FSMs derived from the instruction set, or microcoded, where each instruction maps to a sequence of microinstructions stored in a ROM and the control signals are read from it. Microcode is easier to change and suits complex instruction sets; hardwired control is faster and suits RISC designs and accelerators.

For verification, the split matters too. Datapath bugs are usually data-dependent (overflow, a wrong bit width) and suit word-level and arithmetic reasoning; control bugs are sequence-dependent (a missed stall, a wrong state) and suit model checking and coverage of FSM transitions. Tools for each, and their capacity limits, follow this boundary.

## Going deeper

label: The processor performance equation
lesson:
# The processor performance equation

Execution time factors into instruction count, cycles per instruction (CPI) and clock period. Every microarchitecture and implementation decision moves one of these terms, often at the expense of another, and the equation is how the effect of a timing closure result (a faster clock) is weighed against the effect of an architectural choice (fewer stalls). Amdahl's law bounds what any single improvement can buy.

## Time equals count times CPI times period

$$T_{exec} = IC \times CPI \times T_{clk} = \frac{IC \times CPI}{f}.$$

A program of $2 \times 10^{9}$ instructions with CPI 1.4 on a 2.5 GHz clock takes $2\times10^9 \cdot 1.4 / 2.5\times10^9 = 1.12$ s. The three factors belong to different owners: the compiler and instruction set fix $IC$, the microarchitecture fixes $CPI$, and the circuit implementation and timing closure fix $f$. A deeper pipeline raises $f$ but usually raises $CPI$ through more stall cycles, so only the product decides.

## CPI from an instruction mix

Different instruction classes take different numbers of cycles. The average CPI is the frequency-weighted mean:

$$CPI = \sum_k f_k \cdot CPI_k.$$

With 50% ALU instructions at 1 cycle, 30% loads and stores at 2 cycles and 20% branches at 3 cycles, $CPI = 0.5 + 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.7$. Measurements of CPI by class come from simulation or hardware counters on representative workloads; architectural simulators such as gem5 produce exactly these numbers before any RTL exists.

## Amdahl's law

If an improvement speeds up a fraction $p$ of the execution time by a factor $s$ and leaves the rest unchanged, the overall speedup is

$$S = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + p/s}.$$

Accelerating 60% of the time by a factor of 10 gives $1 / (0.4 + 0.06) \approx 2.17$, far below 10, and even an infinite $s$ caps the speedup at $1/(1 - p) = 2.5$. The same law governs EDA flows: parallelizing a router step that is 70% of runtime across many cores cannot make the flow more than about 3.3 times faster, which is why serial bottlenecks such as timing updates draw so much engineering attention.

## Going deeper

Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (6th ed., 2017), chapter 1; Amdahl, "Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities" (AFIPS, 1967).

label: Pipelining
lesson:
# Pipelining

Pipelining splits a long combinational computation into stages separated by registers, so several operations are in flight at once. The clock period shrinks to the slowest stage plus register overhead, throughput rises, and latency rises slightly. It is the most important timing technique in digital design, used in processors, DSP datapaths and accelerators, and retiming tools automate the placement of pipeline registers.

## Cycle time of a pipeline

Cutting logic into stages with delays $d_1, \dots, d_k$ and inserting a register after each, the clock period is set by the slowest stage plus the register overhead $t_{reg} = t_{cq} + t_{su}$:

$$T_{clk} = \max_i d_i + t_{reg}.$$

Logic of 900 ps split into stages of 250, 200, 300 and 150 ps, with $t_{reg} = 50$ ps, runs at $T_{clk} = 350$ ps instead of $900 + 50 = 950$ ps unpipelined. The imbalance matters: the 300 ps stage sets the clock, and the 150 ps stage wastes half its cycle. Ideal balancing would give $900/4 + 50 = 275$ ps.

## Latency and throughput

A $k$-stage pipeline finishes its first result after $k$ cycles (latency $k\, T_{clk}$) and then one result per cycle. Processing $N$ items takes

$$T_N = (k + N - 1)\, T_{clk}.$$

With $k = 4$ and $T_{clk} = 350$ ps, one item takes 1400 ps, longer than the 950 ps unpipelined, but 1000 items take $1003 \cdot 350 = 351050$ ps, about 351 ns, against 950 ns unpipelined. Throughput approaches $1/T_{clk}$ as $N$ grows; latency is always worse. Which one matters depends on the workload: a streaming filter cares about throughput, a dependent loop cares about latency.

## Speedup and its limits

The speedup on $N$ items is the unpipelined time over the pipelined time, $N (D + t_{reg}) / ((k + N - 1) T_{clk})$, where $D$ is the total logic delay. For the example with $N = 1000$, $950000 / 351050 \approx 2.71$, well below the 4 a naive count suggests, because of imbalance and register overhead.

Deeper pipelines have diminishing returns. As $k$ grows, $T_{clk} \to D/k + t_{reg}$ approaches $t_{reg}$, so speedup saturates near $(D + t_{reg})/t_{reg}$; clock skew and the hazards of the next topic eat further into the gain. Retiming moves registers across logic to balance stages without changing behavior, and an HLS tool chooses the number of stages from the target clock period.

## Going deeper

Harris and Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture" (2nd ed., 2012), section 3.6; Leiserson and Saxe, "Retiming Synchronous Circuitry" (Algorithmica, 1991).

label: Pipeline hazards and stalls
lesson:
# Pipeline hazards and stalls

In a processor pipeline, instructions depend on each other, and a dependent instruction may need a value its predecessor has not yet written. These data hazards, together with structural and control hazards, force the pipeline to stall or to forward values. Counting stall cycles for a code sequence is the core exercise of pipeline design, and the interlock and forwarding logic is a classic target for formal verification.

## The five-stage pipeline and data hazards

The classic RISC pipeline has stages IF (fetch), ID (decode and register read), EX (ALU), MEM (data memory) and WB (register write). Instruction $j$ reads its sources in ID; instruction $i$ writes its result in WB, three cycles after its own ID. With the register file written in the first half of a cycle and read in the second, a reader may sit in ID in the same cycle as the writer is in WB.

Without forwarding, a dependent instruction must therefore reach ID no earlier than 3 cycles after its producer's ID. Back-to-back dependent instructions (distance 1) stall 2 cycles; at distance 2 they stall 1; at distance 3 or more, none. A stall delays the instruction and everything behind it, which changes later distances.

## Forwarding and the load-use hazard

Forwarding routes the ALU result from the EX/MEM or MEM/WB pipeline register straight to the ALU inputs, so a dependent ALU instruction can use a result in the cycle right after it is computed, with no stall. A load is different: its data appears only at the end of MEM, so an instruction that uses a load result immediately must stall 1 cycle (the load-use hazard) and then receive the value by forwarding.

Count total cycles for `lw r1, 0(r2)`, `add r3, r1, r4`, `sub r5, r3, r1`. With forwarding: the add stalls 1 cycle on r1; the sub then forwards r3 with no stall. Three instructions take $5 + 2 = 7$ cycles without stalls, plus 1: 8 cycles. Without forwarding: the add stalls 2 cycles, and the sub, now at distance 1 from the add, stalls 2 more, giving 11 cycles.

## Structural and control hazards

A structural hazard arises when two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle: one memory port shared by fetch and a load, or a register file with too few write ports. The fix is duplication (separate instruction and data caches) or a stall.

A control hazard arises at branches: the pipeline does not know the next fetch address until the branch resolves. If it resolves in EX, two wrongly fetched instructions must be flushed when the branch is taken, a 2-cycle penalty. Hazard detection is a small amount of logic with a large state space (every combination of instructions in flight), which is why processor verification uses formal methods on the interlock and forwarding control, and why compilers schedule independent instructions into the delay slots that hazards create.

## Going deeper

Patterson and Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design" (RISC-V ed., 2017), sections 4.6 to 4.8; Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (6th ed., 2017), appendix C.

label: Branch penalties and prediction
lesson:
# Branch penalties and prediction

Branches are about one instruction in five, and every mispredicted branch flushes the work fetched behind it. Branch predictors guess the outcome early, and the simplest dynamic ones are tiny finite-state machines per branch. Their accuracy, multiplied by the pipeline's flush penalty, is a large term in CPI, and predictor state machines are a neat place where FSM design, microarchitecture and performance arithmetic meet.

## The CPI cost of branches

If a fraction $f_b$ of instructions are branches, a fraction $m$ of those are mispredicted, and each misprediction costs $P$ cycles of flushed work, then

$$CPI = CPI_{base} + f_b \cdot m \cdot P.$$

With $CPI_{base} = 1$, $f_b = 0.2$, $m = 0.1$ and $P = 3$: $CPI = 1.06$. Deep pipelines resolve branches late, so $P$ can be 15 or more cycles in high-frequency cores, and the same 10% misprediction rate then costs $0.2 \cdot 0.1 \cdot 15 = 0.3$ cycles per instruction. That is why predictor accuracy improved from roughly 90% to well above 95% as pipelines deepened.

## The two-bit saturating counter

A 2-bit predictor is a four-state counter per branch: 0 and 1 predict not taken, 2 and 3 predict taken. A taken outcome increments (saturating at 3), not taken decrements (saturating at 0). Two wrong outcomes in a row are needed to flip a strong prediction.

Start at state 1 (weakly not taken) and feed outcomes T, T, N, T, T, T, N, T. The predictions are N, T, T, T, T, T, T, T, and the states after each outcome are 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 3, 2, 3. Mispredictions occur on the first T (predicted N) and the two N outcomes: 3 of 8. The counter is a Moore machine whose output is its prediction.

## One bit versus two bits on loops

A 1-bit predictor simply repeats the last outcome. On a loop branch taken $k - 1$ times then not taken once, repeated, it mispredicts twice per loop execution after the first: once at the exit (predicted taken) and once at the next entry (it remembered not taken). The 2-bit counter mispredicts only at the exit, since one not-taken outcome moves it from 3 to 2, still predicting taken.

For a loop of 4 iterations executed 3 times (outcome pattern TTTN repeated), starting from not taken, a 1-bit predictor mispredicts 6 times (the first T, then each of the first two exits and the re-entry after it, then the final exit: 1 + 2 + 2 + 1), and a 2-bit counter starting at state 1 mispredicts 4 times. Modern predictors (gshare, TAGE) index counters by global history to capture correlations, but the saturating counter remains their basic cell.

## Going deeper

Smith, "A Study of Branch Prediction Strategies" (ISCA, 1981); McFarling, "Combining Branch Predictors" (DEC WRL Technical Note TN-36, 1993); Seznec and Michaud, "A Case for (Partially) Tagged Geometric History Length Branch Prediction" (JILP, 2006).

label: Cache organization and address fields
prereqs: Writing a number in another base
lesson:
# Cache organization and address fields

A cache is an SRAM data array plus a tag array that remembers which memory blocks it holds. Its organization (capacity, block size, associativity) splits every address into tag, index and offset fields and fixes the size of both arrays. These numbers decide the memory macros a physical designer must place, the comparators on the critical path, and the hit rate the architecture sees.

## Tag, index and offset

A cache of capacity $C$ bytes with block (line) size $B$ bytes and associativity $a$ has $C / B$ lines in $S = C/(B a)$ sets. A byte address of $A$ bits splits as

- offset: $\log_2 B$ bits, the byte within the block;
- index: $\log_2 S$ bits, the set;
- tag: $A - \log_2 S - \log_2 B$ bits, stored to identify the block.

A 32 KB, 4-way cache with 64-byte blocks and 32-bit addresses has $32768 / (64 \cdot 4) = 128$ sets: 6 offset bits, 7 index bits and $32 - 7 - 6 = 19$ tag bits.

## Associativity changes the split

For fixed capacity and block size, doubling the associativity halves the number of sets, removes one index bit and adds one tag bit. The same 32 KB cache with 64-byte blocks has 512 sets when direct-mapped (9 index bits, 17 tag bits), 128 sets when 4-way, and 1 set when fully associative (0 index bits, 26 tag bits).

Higher associativity reduces conflict misses, but every way needs a tag comparator active on each access and a wider way-select mux, so hit time and energy rise. A fully associative cache is a CAM. This is why first-level caches stay at modest associativity (often 4 to 8 ways) and large last-level caches use more.

## Total storage

Each line stores its data ($8B$ bits), its tag, a valid bit and, for a write-back cache, a dirty bit. With $L = C/B$ lines,

$$\text{bits} = L \cdot (8B + \text{tag} + 1 + 1).$$

For the 32 KB, 4-way, 64-byte write-back cache: 512 lines of $512 + 19 + 2 = 533$ bits, 272896 bits in total, about 4.1% more than the data alone. Replacement state (LRU bits) adds a little more per set. In the physical design the data and tag arrays are separate SRAM macros, often with the tag array accessed first or in parallel, and their shapes come straight from this arithmetic.

## Going deeper

Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (6th ed., 2017), appendix B; Smith, "Cache Memories" (ACM Computing Surveys, 1982).

label: Cache hits, misses and AMAT
prereqs: Expectation of a function of a random variable
lesson:
# Cache hits, misses and AMAT

A cache's value is measured by how often it hits and how much a miss costs. Average memory access time combines the two, and tracing an address stream through a small cache shows where misses come from: cold starts, limited capacity, and conflicts between addresses that share a set. These traces are what cache simulators compute, and the misses they count become CPI.

## Average memory access time

With hit time $t_h$, miss rate $m$ and miss penalty $t_p$,

$$AMAT = t_h + m \cdot t_p.$$

A 1-cycle L1 with a 5% miss rate and a 100-cycle penalty gives $AMAT = 6$ cycles. With an L2 the penalty itself becomes an access time: $AMAT = t_{h1} + m_1 (t_{h2} + m_2 t_{mem})$. With $t_{h2} = 10$, local L2 miss rate 20% and $t_{mem} = 100$: $1 + 0.05 (10 + 20) = 2.5$ cycles. Small changes in L1 miss rate matter a great deal, because they multiply the whole lower hierarchy.

## Tracing a direct-mapped cache

In a direct-mapped cache with $S$ sets of $B$-byte blocks, byte address $x$ belongs to block $\lfloor x / B \rfloor$, which maps to set $\lfloor x / B \rfloor \bmod S$. Each set holds one block; an access hits if that set already holds its block, otherwise it misses and replaces the set's block.

With 4 sets of 16 bytes, trace addresses 0, 4, 16, 64, 0, 20, 68: blocks 0, 0, 1, 4, 0, 1, 4 in sets 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0. Results: miss (cold), hit, miss (cold), miss (block 4 evicts block 0 from set 0), miss (block 0 evicts block 4), hit, miss. Two hits in seven. Blocks 0 and 4 conflict in set 0 even though the cache has empty sets: conflict misses.

## Associativity and LRU

A 2-way set-associative cache of the same capacity has 2 sets of 2 blocks each, with least-recently-used replacement within a set. The same trace maps blocks 0, 0, 1, 4, 0, 1, 4 to sets 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0. Set 0 can now hold blocks 0 and 4 together: miss, hit, miss, miss, hit, hit, hit. Four hits in seven.

Associativity removed the conflict misses, but it cannot remove cold misses (first touches) or capacity misses (a working set larger than the cache). Cache simulators classify misses into these three categories, and architects tune size, block size and associativity against the hit-time and energy costs from the organization topic. The same trace-driven method, at scale, decides the cache configuration a memory compiler is asked to build.

## Going deeper

Hennessy and Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach" (6th ed., 2017), chapter 2 and appendix B; Hill and Smith, "Evaluating Associativity in CPU Caches" (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1989).

label: Spec-to-RTL agent loops
lesson:
# Spec-to-RTL agent loops

Language models can now write plausible RTL from a plain-language specification. Plausible is not correct. An agent-first front-end flow wraps generation in a harness loop: the model proposes RTL, tools compile, lint, simulate and formally check it against golden references, and failures go back to the model. This concept applies the harness loop to RTL generation for the circuits of this domain.

## The loop for RTL

The harness loop for RTL has the same shape as for engine code: a request arrives ("a 4-deep synchronous FIFO with full and empty flags"), the model proposes RTL, and the harness runs cheap checks first and expensive ones later. Parse and elaborate (a Verilog front end such as Yosys or Verilator), lint (latches, width mismatches, combinational loops, multiple drivers), simulate against a test bench, check properties formally, and synthesize to see area and timing. Each failure is turned into feedback the model can act on: the line of a lint warning, the first failing cycle of a waveform, a formal counterexample trace.

The loop ends with a reviewable diff and its evidence, not with "the model says it works".

## Golden references for small circuits

For the circuits in this domain, golden references are unusually strong. A combinational block with up to about 20 inputs can be checked exhaustively in simulation. An adder or multiplier can be checked against the language's own arithmetic operator by a combinational equivalence checker, regardless of architecture. An FSM can be checked against a reference machine by sequential equivalence from reset, or against temporal properties ("full and empty are never both asserted").

The agent should prefer checks that are complete over checks that sample: a passing random test bench says little about a corner such as the most negative two's-complement value, whereas an equivalence proof covers every input.

## Where the loop fails

The loop inherits the weaknesses of its checks. If the specification is ambiguous (overlapping or non-overlapping detection, which reset value, signed or unsigned comparison), the model may pick one reading, the test bench another, and the loop will either thrash or converge on the test bench's reading. If the test bench is weak, the model can pass it without implementing the specification.

So the harness should surface ambiguities as questions to the human rather than resolve them silently, keep the golden reference independent of the model's own output (a model-written test bench checking model-written RTL proves little), and record each confirmed specification decision so the next request starts from it.

## Going deeper

The Yosys, Verilator and SymbiYosys documentation; Thakur et al., "VeriGen: A Large Language Model for Verilog Code Generation" (ACM TODAES, 2024); Liu et al., "VerilogEval: Evaluating Large Language Models for Verilog Code Generation" (ICCAD, 2023).

A) Rare corner cases such as the most negative value may not have been hit

B) The adder must be wrong since it passed so quickly

C) Random tests always miss overflow

D) Nothing, a million vectors is exhaustive for 16 bits
problems.a: Rare corner cases such as the most negative value may not have been hit
problems.e: Two 16-bit operands give about four billion pairs; a million random ones sample a small fraction, so corners need directed tests or a formal check.

problems.q:
The model writes both the RTL and the testbench that checks it. What is the weakness?

A) Testbenches cannot be generated by models

B) Lint cannot check testbench code

C) The simulation will run too slowly

D) Both can share the same misunderstanding, so the test passes a wrong design
problems.a: Both can share the same misunderstanding, so the test passes a wrong design
problems.e: A golden reference must be independent of the generated design, or a shared mistake goes undetected.

problems.q:
The spec says 'detect 1011' and does not say whether overlapping matches count. What should the agent do?

A) Pick overlapping silently, since it is more common

B) Generate both and submit whichever passes its own testbench

C) Ask the human which reading is intended and record the answer

D) Leave the ambiguity in a code comment
problems.a: Ask the human which reading is intended and record the answer
problems.e: An ambiguous spec lets the RTL and the testbench disagree; resolving it with the human prevents converging on the wrong reading.

problems.q:
A confirmed spec decision (reset value, signedness) should be kept where?

A) In a recorded specification the next request starts from

B) Only in the model's conversation context

C) Nowhere; each request should start fresh

D) In a comment inside the generated RTL alone
problems.a: In a recorded specification the next request starts from
problems.e: Recording decisions avoids re-asking and keeps later generated blocks consistent.

label: Golden and differential checks for generated RTL
lesson:
# Golden and differential checks for generated RTL

When an agent changes RTL, two questions need evidence: is the new design correct against the specification (golden), and did it change only what was intended (differential)? Digital logic offers unusually sharp instruments for both: combinational and sequential equivalence checking, exhaustive simulation for small blocks, and QoR comparisons after synthesis. Knowing what each instrument proves is the difference between a trusted agent and a plausible one.

## What each check proves

- **Directed or random simulation** shows the design behaves correctly on the vectors run, and nothing about the rest. Exhaustive simulation of an $n$-input combinational block needs $2^n$ vectors: fine at 16 inputs, hopeless at 64.
- **Combinational equivalence checking** proves that two netlists with matching registers compute the same next-state and output functions for every input, using SAT and structural hashing. It is the standard check after synthesis.
- **Sequential equivalence checking** proves two designs produce the same outputs from reset for every input sequence, even when their registers differ (retiming, re-encoded FSMs).
- **Property checking** proves stated properties hold, which is only as strong as the properties.

## Differential checks for an edit

For a refactoring edit (re-encoding an FSM, replacing a ripple adder by a prefix adder, retiming a pipeline) the right check is equivalence against the previous version: behavior must not change at all. For a functional edit (add a saturate mode, change a reset value) equivalence must fail, and the check becomes: equivalent under the old mode, and the new behavior matches the specification under the new one. Constrain the comparison to the unchanged modes and prove those equivalent.

On top of correctness, a differential QoR report after synthesis (area, worst slack, cell count, power estimate) shows whether the edit had the intended physical effect, and nothing else moved.

## Pitfalls

Equivalence checkers need a correspondence or a reset state, and both can hide problems. Two FSMs equivalent from reset can differ from an illegal state, which matters if the specification requires safe recovery. A design that is equivalent only because both versions share the same bug (both copied from one wrong reference) passes every differential check; that is why the golden reference must be independent.

Don't-care handling is another trap: synthesis may exploit X assignments differently in the two versions, so an equivalence check that treats X as a free choice can pass designs that simulate differently. A trustworthy harness states its X semantics and its reset assumptions alongside every pass.

## Going deeper

Kuehlmann and Krohm, "Equivalence Checking Using Cuts and Heaps" (DAC, 1997); Mishchenko et al., "Improvements to Combinational Equivalence Checking" (ICCAD, 2006); the ABC documentation for cec and dsec.

problems.q:
A retimed pipeline moved registers across logic. Which check can prove it still matches the original?

A) Sequential equivalence checking

B) A static timing report

C) Combinational equivalence with name matching

D) Lint
problems.a: Sequential equivalence checking
problems.e: Retiming breaks register correspondence, so equivalence must be proved over sequences from reset.

problems.q:
What does a passing directed testbench prove about a design?

A) That it matches the specification

B) That it is equivalent to the previous version

C) That it is correct for all inputs

D) That it behaves correctly on the vectors applied, and nothing more
problems.a: That it behaves correctly on the vectors applied, and nothing more
problems.e: Simulation is evidence on the tested inputs only; completeness needs exhaustive or formal methods.

problems.q:
Two netlists have the same registers, matched by name. Which check proves they compute the same functions?

A) Random simulation

B) Combinational equivalence checking

C) Sequential equivalence checking from reset

D) A QoR comparison
problems.a: Combinational equivalence checking
problems.e: With corresponding registers, equivalence reduces to proving every next-state and output function equal, a combinational problem.

problems.q:
An agent adds a saturate mode to an adder, enabled by a new input. How is the edit checked?

A) Require full equivalence with the old design

B) Prove equivalence with the old design when saturate is off, and check the new behavior when it is on

C) Only check the synthesized area

D) Skip equivalence because behavior changed
problems.a: Prove equivalence with the old design when saturate is off, and check the new behavior when it is on
problems.e: Constraining equivalence to the unchanged mode proves nothing else moved, while the new mode is checked against the spec.

problems.q:
An agent replaces a ripple adder with a Brent-Kung adder as a pure refactor. What must the differential check show?

A) That the testbench still compiles

B) That some outputs changed, proving the edit took effect

C) Only that the new design synthesizes

D) Full equivalence with the previous version, plus the intended QoR change
problems.a: Full equivalence with the previous version, plus the intended QoR change
problems.e: A refactor must not change behavior at all, and the QoR diff shows the intended timing and area effect.

problems.q:
After an FSM re-encoding, a differential QoR report shows area down 8% and worst slack unchanged. What else must hold before accepting it?

A) Nothing; the QoR improved

B) Sequential equivalence from reset with the original

C) An identical netlist

D) A larger flip-flop count
problems.a: Sequential equivalence from reset with the original
problems.e: QoR shows the physical effect, but correctness needs its own proof.

problems.q:
What should a trustworthy harness report alongside every equivalence pass?

A) Its reset assumptions and its treatment of X and don't-cares

B) Only the runtime of the check

C) The number of lines changed

D) The model's confidence score
problems.a: Its reset assumptions and its treatment of X and don't-cares
problems.e: Those assumptions define what the proof covers; without them a reviewer cannot judge its strength.

problems.q:
Both the old and new versions of a block were derived from the same flawed reference model. What will the differential check show?

A) A failure at the bug's location

B) A pass, because both share the same bug

C) A QoR regression

D) A lint error
problems.a: A pass, because both share the same bug
problems.e: Differential checks prove sameness, not correctness; an independent golden reference is needed to catch a shared bug.

problems.q:
Synthesis is free to choose values for X assignments. Why can that make an equivalence pass misleading?

A) X values are always resolved to 0 by every tool

B) X assignments are illegal in synthesizable RTL

C) Equivalence checkers reject any design containing X

D) The two versions may resolve X differently and simulate differently, while the checker treats X as a free choice
problems.a: The two versions may resolve X differently and simulate differently, while the checker treats X as a free choice
problems.e: The X semantics of the check must be stated, or a pass may hide behavior differences that simulation would show.
